summary: This Wikipedia article traces the Huguenots, French Protestants whose persecution, especially after the revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685, drove large-scale emigration to the Dutch Republic, Britain, Prussia, North America, South Africa and Brazil. It covers their settlements in New Netherland, Charleston and Virginia, the Montpellier ville de sûreté, the Wars of Religion, the Camisard revolt, and debated origins of the name Huguenot.
one_line: Overview of the French Huguenots, their persecution, emigration to Europe and the Americas, and the disputed origin of their name.
key_facts: After the revocation of the Edict of Nantes, the Dutch Republic received the largest group of Huguenot refugees, an estimated 75,000 to 100,000 people.
Around 1700, it is estimated that nearly 25% of the Amsterdam population was Huguenot.
In 1705, Amsterdam and the area of West Frisia were the first areas to provide full citizens rights to Huguenot immigrants, followed by the Dutch Republic in 1715.
Huguenots led by Jessé de Forest sailed to North America in 1624 after being barred from settling in New France, and settled in the Dutch colony of New Netherland.
In 1628 the Huguenots established a congregation called L'Église française à la Nouvelle-Amsterdam, which continues today as L'Eglise du Saint-Esprit, part of the Episcopal (Anglican) communion.
The revocation of the Edict of Nantes forbade Protestant services, required education of children as Catholics, and prohibited emigration.
Four thousand Huguenots emigrated to the North American colonies, where they settled in New York and Virginia, especially.

Pierre Bayle, one of the most prominent Huguenot refugees in the Netherlands, published his multi-volume Historical and Critical Dictionary, which became one of the 100 foundational texts of the US Library of Congress.
Montpellier was among the 66 'villes de sûreté' granted to the Huguenots by the Edict of 1598, and Protestant rule there was dead by the Edict of Alès (1629).
Huguenot numbers peaked near an estimated two million by 1562, about one-eighth the number of French Catholics.
The Wars of Religion were fought intermittently from 1562 to 1598 and ended with the granting of the Edict of Nantes.
In 1685, Louis XIV issued the Edict of Fontainebleau, revoking the Edict of Nantes and declaring Protestantism illegal.
A group of Huguenots arrived in Brazil in 1555 to found France Antarctique and built Fort Coligny, which the Portuguese destroyed in 1560.
Maria de la Queillerie, wife of commander Jan van Riebeeck, was the first Huguenot to arrive at the Cape of Good Hope, on 6 April 1652.
On 12 May 1705, the Virginia General Assembly passed an act to naturalise the 148 Huguenots still resident at Manakintown.

entities.role: 1598 edict granting Huguenots religious, political and military autonomy, later revoked in 1685

entities.role: 1685 edict that revoked the Edict of Nantes and declared Protestantism illegal

entities.role: French king who acted increasingly aggressively to force Huguenots to convert

entities.role: country that received the largest group of Huguenot refugees after the revocation

entities.role: Dutch colony where Huguenots settled after 1624

entities.role: parish descended from the 1628 Huguenot congregation in New Amsterdam, part of the Episcopal (Anglican) communion

entities.name: Pierre Bayle

entities.role: multi-volume work by Pierre Bayle, one of the 100 foundational texts of the US Library of Congress
